utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic, Simo Zaric, case number IT-95-9-PT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Nancy Paterson representing of the Office of the Prosecutor, and with me is case manager Diane Boles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Deyan Brashich for the Todorovic Defence. I'm joined at the counsel table by Nikola Kostich. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a hearing under Rule 62 bis, and its purpose is to have the Chamber determine whether it is satisfied as to the four matters set out in that Rule so that it may enter a finding of guilt on the basis of the accused Todorovic's guilty plea made on December 13, 2000. If the Chamber determines that a finding of guilt is to be entered, it will then set a date for the sentence hearing. The matters in respect of which the Chamber must be satisfied, if it is to enter a finding of guilt, are that the plea is voluntary, that it is informed, it is not equivocal, and that there is a sufficient factual basis for it as well as of the accused's participation in the crime. We have before us a document filed jointly by the Prosecutor and the Defence, setting out the factual basis for the charges in respect of which the accused has pleaded guilty. Judge Hunt has one or two questions in relation to the factual basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, perhaps you would be able to assist me. The agreement which has been signed admits expressly all of the relevant facts alleged against the accused in the indictment except 34(A) and (B), and there is no express admission in terms of the crime alleged in 36 -- I'm sorry, 29 and 30. Now, I realise that this is a joint submission, this factual basis for the charges, and it seems to me, having read through them, I might add with some difficulty because it's very difficult to find your way through it, there is certainly a factual basis there for each of 34(A) and (B). The way in which the Prosecution has pleaded the indictment is that if it has established all of the ingredients of paragraph 34 plus 40 to 47, which are all admitted, then it has established the crime alleged in paragraph 29. I'm curious, first, as to why we have to rely upon all this extraneous material, there being no express admission to it, because the Rule seems to contemplate that there must be no dispute between the parties in relation to the fundamental matters upon which the plea is based. Is there any significance in the fact that the agreement has not expressly admitted those matters in 34(A) and (B)?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. As you know, this is, as far as I know, only the third plea that has taken place before the Tribunal, so the procedure to be followed is still somewhat new to all of us. This submission was based on the previous submissions provided to this Court in the earlier pleas and was, as stated, the result of negotiations between Mr. Brashich and myself. I could have obviously put in more information; I purposely limited the information so that Mr. Brashich and I could reach an agreement. I do believe that there is sufficient information in here to support all of the subparagraphs -- subsections in paragraph 34. If you read through the extracts that we provided, most of them cover many different crimes in one statement. So that while they will talk about the murder, the murder took place in the police station which was a detention centre, and people were being beaten at the same time that the murder happened. So it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That -- I'm pausing for the purposes of the translators. That is actually expressly admitted elsewhere in the agreement. But what I'm concerned about, and it's only a passing concern but I thought I have to be satisfied so I'd raise it with you, is the fact that this document which has been tendered as a joint submission by both parties, does the Prosecution understand that as an admission by Mr. Todorovic of the facts which are asserted in paragraphs 34(A) and 34(B)? I'm going to ask Mr. Brashich the same question but I thought I'd start off with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do look at that as an admission on Mr. Todorovic's part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If that's so, then I'm satisfied. But I just wanted to know from both parties, seeing it wasn't in the express agreement, that's all. Well, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Was the intention of this joint filing of the factual basis for the charges to amount to an admission by your client that those facts establish the allegations in paragraphs 34(A) and (B) of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was negotiated by myself with Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't want to know the details of the negotiation, obviously. But the fact that it wasn't expressly contained in the agreement just put me on warning. I am happy to accept your assurance as counsel that your client accepts that those facts do establish paragraphs 34(A) and 34(B) of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Because of the negotiations, things were done sometimes in a hurried manner in order to meet certain deadlines, so perhaps we did not dot the i's and cross the t's. We were under severe time constraints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand fully. I am not very familiar with plea-bargaining in the country from which I come, but, nevertheless, it's been an interesting exercise to see the results from it. Thank you. You have satisfied me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that matter having been clarified, I will now ask the accused, Mr. Todorovic, certain questions in relation to the matters in respect of which we have to be satisfied under Rule 62 bis. Will you stand, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you entered into a plea agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor and, pursuant to that agreement, you pleaded guilty on the 13th of December, 2000 to the first count of the indictment, charging persecutions as a crime against humanity. In accordance with that agreement, you will withdraw all motions before the Chamber challenging the legality of your arrest and seeking judicial assistance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pursuant to that agreement, the Prosecutor and the Defence have recommended to the Chamber that the sentence falls within the range of five to 12 years. You must understand, however, that the sentence is ultimately a matter for the Chamber to determine, in accordance with the Statute and the Rules, and that this may be for a term up to and including life imprisonment. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you discussed fully with your counsel the plea agreement that you have made with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you threatened or coerced in any way to make that agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not threatened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you threatened or coerced in any way to enter a plea of guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have made that plea voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you discussed the matter fully with your counsel, and has he informed you of the nature of the charges against you and of the consequences of pleading guilty to a crime against humanity?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson and Mr. Brashich, at the first hearing, we discussed the question of the withdrawal by the Prosecution of all of the counts, a withdrawal by the Defence of all motions relating to the evidentiary hearing and the legality of the arrest. The Chamber will accept an assurance given today by both counsel about these matters that the withdrawal will be effective as of today. You will, however, confirm it in writing within a week. So I ask first Ms. Paterson: Does the Office of the Prosecutor give the assurance that it will withdraw all of the counts, that is, counts other than Count 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As part of the agreement, a copy of which has been provided to the Court, it is quite clear that it is the intention of the Office of the Prosecutor to withdraw Counts 2 to 27. I would just like to point out that part of the reason we agreed to that is our feeling that the persecution count, by its nature, essentially encompasses the same allegations made in those counts, so that for the sake of the witnesses and victims involved in those counts, they can hopefully see that their interests are, nonetheless, being protected by this plea. But yes, I can state that it is our intention to withdraw those counts and, as you requested, I will do so in writing within a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brashich, do you give the assurance that you withdraw all motions relating to the evidentiary hearing and those questioning the legality of arrest?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Before I do that, Your Honour, I want to make it clear, and I would request of Ms. Paterson to make the withdrawal with prejudice, that it not be just a plain withdrawal. It has to be a withdrawal with prejudice. And if the withdrawal is with prejudice, I will, in writing, withdraw all pending motions before the Trial Chambers and make a representation as called for in writing by paragraph 8 of the plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it was not a part of the negotiated plea that we would withdraw those counts with prejudice. I will state that if, as Your Honours say, you will accept this plea - and I see no problems with the plea being accepted - that once this hearing is concluded, we will agree to do that. However, I think Mr. Brashich must admit that that was not part of the negotiation, but for sake of proceeding with this agreement, I am willing to take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Your Honour, as I had stated before, I will readily admit that I did not cross t's and dot the i's. The thought with regard to "with prejudice" came to me as I was sitting, listening to Your Honour question Ms. Paterson. I do not wish to be in a position of being sandbagged, where my client has given up some rather valuable rights to have the indictment reinstated, if I have to, and I do readily admit that this is not the first or perhaps the last misstep or mistake that I might have made before this Trial Chamber. However, it was clearly the intent on the part of the Defence to give up certain rights and receive certain benefits, and one of the benefits is the dismissal of 26 counts. So I would call upon Ms. Paterson to live up to the spirit and the intent of the agreement and withdraw the 26 counts with prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, I think what Mr. Brashich is saying that the clear intent of the agreement was that the other counts would not be brought again against his client, and what he wants is a firm assurance that those counts will be withdrawn and will not be brought again against his client.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: What I can state, Your Honour, is that we are fully prepared to live up to our side of the agreement. I will file in writing a statement this week stating that we are withdrawing the remaining counts. Assuming that the agreement is concluded to the satisfaction of all parties that Mr. Todorovic lives up to his side of the agreement, then of course we have absolutely no intention of ever reinstating these charges, but I am not prepared today to withdraw them with prejudice. If for some reason the agreement falls through, Mr. Todorovic does not live up to his part of the agreement, then obviously we need to return to square one and proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, this raises a vital issue that has yet to be resolved about this agreement. The agreement appears to contemplate that Mr. Todorovic will not be sentenced until he has fulfilled all his obligations under the agreement, one of which is to give evidence against other people, including his co-accused. That in itself is a very real problem because if he does give his evidence before he is sentenced, then there will be an even greater attack upon the credibility of that evidence, that he is inflating his evidence or lying in order to get a greater degree of mitigation. Now, if you are also going to hold over his head this issue of prejudice so that it's up to the Prosecution to be satisfied that he has given evidence, et cetera, you are going -- are you not going to destroy a great deal of the credibility of the evidence which he is going to give in these other trials? And if I may add another matter that you should consider. Having conceded that this count of persecution is going to include all of the factual matter that's in that indictment, you will surely face an application for a stay of any further indictment you may try to bring on the basis it's an abuse of process.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was not our intention that Mr. Todorovic should not be sentenced until he complies with all aspects of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: The agreement anticipates that this understanding could potentially go on for years. We don't know how many trials there may be that he might be asked to testify at, how long this will take. It is our assumption that he would actually be sentenced in the relatively near future and that we would then proceed in good faith, with the understanding that if at some point in the future he fails to live up to that, to his part of the agreement, we will have to come back, revisit the issue, and consider the appropriate resolution at that time. But we did not intend that he not be sentenced, and we had no intention whatsoever of holding any counts over his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How do you anticipate that it could be resolved in the future if you say that he has, sometime in a few years time, not lived up to his part of the agreement? Is he going to be brought back for resentencing? This is the problem that I see with the way this agreement has been drafted about the sentencing part of it. And you will also have to face up to, will you not, the other matter I raised, and that is that it would be a complete abuse of process, whether it's with or without prejudice, to bring further proceedings based on the same facts. And having had to look at this recently in another context, how do you get over all of that United States authority that was relied upon in Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our intention was simply that we would live up to the agreement, which we felt was quite simple and, I think, was understood as well by Mr. Brashich. I have no reason to think that Mr. Todorovic does not fully intend to live up to his part of the bargain. If, in fact, at some point in time the bargain falls through, whether it is next week or five years from now, the clear understanding of the agreement, as I believe Mr. Brashich and I understand it, is that we all go back to square one again, the indictment is reinstated, the charges proceed against Mr. Todorovic as if the plea had never happened, and we proceed accordingly. This is the way it operates in other jurisdictions and I would assume it would operate that way here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And what happens to the plea itself, the admission made by the plea if the whole proceedings have to restart?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I would assume that the Court would have to rule on that, whether that could be used against him or not. There is obviously precedents in different jurisdictions, but the precedents are somewhat different. I don't know that I'm in a position today to answer that question unequivocally. I believe that would be a decision for the Court to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's precisely what the word "prejudice" means, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I could be heard. I think that Ms. Paterson and I are in agreement with regard to the way that we envisaged the plea and the sentence to take place in a relatively short time so that the plea agreement could be effected, and I believe that we were talking yesterday about a sentence imposed within a period of 60 to 90 days so that the required cooperation would be almost in the immediate future. The reason why I had raised the issue -- I said it came to my mind, the with-prejudice issue, as I was sitting here and listening to Judge Robinson question Ms. Paterson. On the other hand, my co-counsel pointed out to me that in paragraph 6(A) of the agreement, the Prosecutor has accepted the accused's plea to Count 1 in the satisfaction of the remaining counts of the indictment. Had I been redrafting the agreement, and perhaps in the future for other counsel, it should have read: "... in full satisfaction of the remaining counts in the indictment." I might be also guilty of wanting to have both a belt and suspenders for my client, but I want to afford my client the full protection of the intent of the agreement. I did not, in any way, want to derail the agreement that Ms. Paterson and I worked quite intensely to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson and Mr. Brashich --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the Chamber has considered this matter. What we are minded to do is to give the parties half an hour in which to try to resolve this. I would like to say to Ms. Paterson that the Chamber's understanding, certainly based on paragraph 6(A) in particular, the words "the Prosecutor will accept the accused's plea to Count 1 in satisfaction of the remaining counts," is that the Prosecutor would withdraw all the remaining counts and that all those counts would not be brought again. So we are sympathetic and understand the position taken by Mr. Brashich when he asks that the withdrawal be with prejudice. We will give you half an hour in which to try to resolve this matter, and you can seek advice from your appropriate authorities, Ms. Paterson, on this matter. We will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, do you have good news for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. We have conferred with the Prosecution, and I would like to turn over this issue to my co-counsel, Mr. Kostich, to address the Court, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTICH
utterances.text: This sounds like one of the filibusters in the U.S. Senate, because what I'm going to have to do, Your Honour, is to actually ask Ms. Paterson to speak with you. We've had a chance to meet and draft some additional language, which Ms. Paterson will go into, and hopefully we will be able to have that language approved by you. Of course, certainly, you may have some questions. If I may, I would like to pass the torch on to Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The relay continues. Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we discussed this, as you requested, and I think it was somewhat of a -- I don't wish to speak for Defence counsel, but somewhat of a misunderstanding on their part, and obviously they can speak to that when I finish. We've drafted an agreement which is simply two additional sentences, and what I suggest is that I would read this into the record. Then what we can do is add it as a corrigendum to the plea agreement when I also file my written agreement to withdraw the additional counts, and all three of us can sign it so that it would become part of the official record. The additional sentences we have agreed to are: "It is the understanding of the parties that the accused is to fulfil his obligations pursuant to the plea agreement in return of which the Office of the Prosecutor shall withdraw Counts 2 through 27 of the Indictment, in full satisfaction with the accused's plea to Count 1 of the indictment. "Should the accused fail to fulfil his obligations under the plea agreement, it is understood that the Office of the Prosecutor can reinstate the full indictment, including Counts 1 to 27." And there is no language in this agreement concerning prejudice. I think Mr. Kostich can address that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kostich.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have heard the language that we have agreed upon. We have discussed with Mr. Todorovic the language in question. He approves it; Mr. Brashich and I also. We feel satisfied that the language, as indicated by Ms. Paterson, takes care of any concerns that we have. We will no longer insist on a withdrawal with prejudice. We understand that the Office of the Prosecutor has negotiated with us in good faith, and essentially it is an agreement that has been reached. We feel that we can carry out our part of the obligations, and we feel that the Prosecutor's Office will carry out their part of the obligations, and it is, therefore, contemplated that we will sign and enter into this addition, correction to the agreement, and we would withdraw our request for a dismissal with prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I ask you a question about that? The expression "until the Defence fulfils its obligation," has been used, which is the very expression I raised earlier as to what it meant. As an ordinary lawyer, I would read the agreement as saying that the conditions or the obligations are not fulfilled until your client has given evidence, which suggests then that these additional counts will not be withdrawn until he's given evidence. Now, I would like to have it made clear at least between the parties as to whether that was what it was intended. It's contrary now to what Ms. Paterson had said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I don't think it's contrary. The understanding between us is that we will withdraw Counts 2 to 27 as of now. We are assuming that we can proceed with the sentencing in, as suggested, 60 to 90 days, and that we realise that that means that the fulfillment of the agreement will take place in the future. The clear understanding, however, is that at some point in time, if Mr. Todorovic fails to fulfil the agreement, which, as Your Honour knows, involves more than simply testifying at a trial, if the agreement falls through, then we all return to square one as we were before this agreement, which means we can reinstate the entire indictment, Counts 1 to 27. We do not lose the right to bring back Counts 2 to 26 - clearly that's the benefit that we're getting out of the agreement - and we proceed to trial as if there had been no plea agreement and Mr. Todorovic is not prejudiced in any way. The agreement simply dissolves and we proceed as if it had never existed in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You withdraw first and then you reinstate if he doesn't fulfil his obligations. Of course, how a Chamber will view such a reinstatement is perhaps a matter that we need not concern ourselves with here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But I still am concerned, and I'm not merely trying to help the Prosecution, although it may sound like this, I'm trying to take a quite neutral stance about it, but what does the Trial Chamber before whom Mr. Todorovic gives evidence make of that? They will make of it that he is giving evidence with the threat that if he doesn't give evidence in accordance with what the Prosecution expects, he will have these counts reinstated, subject to any Trial Chamber allowing you to do so. What I'm concerned about is what the Trial Chamber who hears his evidence is to make of that evidence received in those circumstances. Now, you may have considered that and you're prepared to take the risk, but if so, I think we should hear you say that so that that Trial Chamber will know precisely how to approach Mr. Todorovic's evidence in those cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but the scenario that we envision is -- the scenario you have just painted is going to be the situation no matter what. If Mr. Todorovic is going to testify at a trial, even if we weren't going to reinstate Counts 2 to 27, he's still going to have the threat of Count 1 hanging over his head that could be reinstated if he fails to comply with the agreement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, because he's been sentenced on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: And if the agreement falls through, if he fails to comply with the agreement, we all go back to where we started, which includes Count 1 and Counts 2 to 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So the Prosecution is prepared to put him forward as a witness who you're going to ask the Trial Chamber to believe that evidence with that hanging over his head in any event. That certainly seems to me to be a very strange situation for the Prosecution to be putting itself in, but if that's what it wants to do, at least we all know that that's what it wants to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, that is the procedure that is followed in other jurisdictions. Obviously, it's up to the Trial Chamber, as you say, to evaluate that. There are many ways that they will have to choose to evaluate the testimony of Mr. Todorovic. That is only one. But, yes, that is the understanding that we're prepared to proceed with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, having heard all the submissions, is satisfied as to the four matters set out in Rule 62 bis: First, that the guilty plea was made voluntarily, that the guilty plea was informed, that it is not equivocal, and that there is a sufficient factual basis for the crime of persecution to which the accused has pleaded guilty and his participation in it. The Chamber enters a finding of guilty on the basis of the guilty plea. There are some other matters that have to be raised. There's the date for sentencing. The Chamber will fix, but only in a provisional way -- Mr. Brashich, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was wondering, in taking the provisional date, the Court would allow a request by the Defence that we do need 60 days to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We had in mind April the 4th. What does your arithmetic make of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: We had been thinking, if it was convenient for the Court, the week of March 19th, and we would suggest that the sentencing phase, at least in consultation with Mr. Kostich and Mr. Todorovic, that we would request of the Court a day, a full trial day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The senior legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, we will certainly take into account the submissions that you have made, but we can't give an assurance. There are various organisational matters to be considered, but we will take account of what you have said, and you will be informed of the date by the senior legal officer, who will, as usual, consult with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Prior to the sentencing hearing, of course, a Scheduling Order will be issued requiring information as to the level of cooperation of the accused with the Prosecution. A Scheduling Order will also be issued seeking submissions on the question of the separation of the proceedings following the accused's guilty plea. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just if I may add, Ms. Paterson, in case this is not the procedure that you're accustomed to, the procedure that I am accustomed to would be that we would be supplied with a statement, signed by Mr. Todorovic, of the evidence that he is going to give. Some of it may obviously be confidential in nature. But we have to judge from the statement the degree of cooperation he's giving in order to assess the proper amount of mitigation. Now, is it contemplated we'll get such a statement, or have you got some other way of telling us what his cooperation has been?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I think that we can probably comply with what you're requesting, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, it's no good stating in general terms that he will cooperate or as it is expressed in the agreement. I think we are obliged to have more detail than that. That's why in my jurisdiction we usually get a statement from the accused of the evidence that he is going to give.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I believe that we'll be able to comply with that requirement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Scheduling Order will address the precise terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just have a moment with Ms. Paterson? Can I just have a moment to speak with Ms. Paterson, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've solved the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just before we adjourn, I had brought to the attention of the Senior Legal Officer that there was one other matter we needed to discuss in a closed session or a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I would join in that respect with regard to closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will go into closed session. The blinds will have to be drawn.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Rule 62 bis Hearing adjourned
